tweets.text:
Inflationary pressures are intensifying in the US manufacturing sector:

The ISM Manufacturing Prices Paid Index surged +6.8 points in September, to 77.9, its highest since May.

This also marks its largest monthly increase since February.

Year-to-date, the index has soared +19.4 points, its third-biggest 9-month increase since 2021.

Meanwhile, the ISM Manufacturing PMI index eased slightly in September by -0.1 point, to 54.5, remaining in expansion for the 9th consecutive month, its longest streak since 2022.

Furthermore, new orders rose +1.6 points, to 55.3, also posting their 9th consecutive monthly expansion.

And, the backlog of unfilled orders jumped +4.6 points, to 56.4, its 2nd-highest level since May 2022.

Manufacturing price pressures are building as elevated demand puts further strain on capacity.

That friction is a national security liability.

Lio co-founder and CEO Vlad Keil on the KPI for the company's forward-deployed engineers: automate your own job, then move to the next one.

"When you look at the org structure of Lio, 85% of the people are engineers."

"And even the people who don't have an engineering title mostly have an engineering background. The reason for that is we don't want to be a consulting company."

"There is a lot of forward-deployed work to do if you go to enterprises because they have different nuances in their processes. But how we work is... building a product in a way where we're reducing this customization, but also where it's a lot of self-service."

"The job of our FDEs is on the one hand making it self-service, but internally it's automating their own job. Their KPI is... literally your job is to automate yourself. And then if you automate yourself, you go to the next task."

@askvladi

tweets.text:
a16z's Seema Amble on why AI-native startups still beat incumbents: the incumbent owns the system of record, the startup owns the whole job.

"Why do you need an AI-native startup if you've got Claudeforce... You've got all your data, and your employees are used to the product. So why another product?"

"I absolutely still think there's a case for the AI-native startup, and it centers around the fact that the legacy incumbent is limited to their system of record, and they're not completing the end-to-end job."

"Say a customer calls and says they got charged after they cancelled. Resolving that isn't just the customer going into the chat and saying 'Hey, I got overcharged.'"

"The response there has to hit billing, it has to look at all the chat history, it has to look at the contract. That's not one system of record, that's the knowledge around that customer and everything it touched."

"The opportunity for the AI-native startup is to say: we're going to own that entire end-to-end arc. That could be legal, owning everything from brief all the way through trial... It's really the concept of owning the end-to-end work."

@seema_amble

ETFs broke the altcoin rotation. @CryptoWithKris says that's why Bitcoin dominance has been flat for over a year.

The old way: you bought Bitcoin on an exchange, every alt was one click away, and gains rotated straight in.

The new way: institutions buy through the ETF, and that money has no path out of the wrapper. It only reaches an alt if the alt has its own ETF, and there are maybe ten of those.

The rotation didn't die. The pipe did.

When money gets scared, it runs to the Swiss franc. This week it sprinted.

EUR-CHF just posted its biggest weekly drop since the April 2025 tariff shock, as French political and fiscal angst hammered the euro. The franc won by default.

Look at the yield. Switzerland pays almost nothing on a zero policy rate, and investors piled into the franc anyway. When people accept zero to hold a currency, they are buying safety, not return.

This is the market's fear gauge, and it just flashed. The French bond stress is leaking into FX.

A franc this strong also runs straight into the SNB, which has intervened before to cap it. Watch for Swiss pushback.

Wall Street is bracing for Brazil.

One-week implied volatility on the real just spiked to about 30%, back toward crisis levels, as a toss-up election looms. Traders are paying up for protection.

The setup underneath is ugly. Brazil's nominal budget deficit has ballooned back to about 9% of GDP, with no pandemic to blame this time. The hole got bigger in good times.

On the surface the currency looks calm. The real has gone roughly nowhere under Lula, around 5.2 per dollar, despite violent swings along the way.

That calm is the setup, not the all-clear. The fiscal hole is the fuel and the election is the match. If you hold EM exposure, Brazil is the binary event on the calendar.

$EWZ

Want to read the Iran war? Follow the oil.

For most of 2026, the fighting choked the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi crude shipments cratered. Riyadh scrambled to reroute barrels west through the Red Sea pipeline instead.

Now it is flipping back. In September, Saudi shipments rose to near their 2025 average as Hormuz transits soared. Saudi also pushed its East-West pipeline above 80% of its 7 million barrel a day capacity.

This is the supply side of the energy squeeze starting to heal. More Saudi barrels hitting the market is what eventually pulls the crude and diesel spike back down.

The barrels are moving again. Watch this chart, not the headlines.

Instead of trading memecoins against stablecoins, people on Robinhood Chain traded them against tokenized stocks, turning shares of Nvidia and AMC into the house chips for speculation.

Grail's stock nearly doubled in a month after an FDA panel backed its Galleri cancer blood test. Investors are betting big.

Look at what the price assumes. Wolfe Research values Grail near $50 without Medicare coverage and near $150 with it. The stock already trades around $150.

So the price treats a Medicare yes as a near-certainty. Wolfe puts the odds closer to a coin flip.

Even a yes pays slowly. Coverage would not start until 2029, and only for ages 50 to 65 at first. Grail is still bleeding hundreds of millions a year, so a capital raise looks almost inevitable.

The real question is not whether the test works, it is whether Medicare pays for it, three years out, with no margin of safety left in the price.

$GRAL

Diesel is the fuel that moves the economy. Right now it is screaming.

US diesel just hit a record $6.52 a gallon, up about 70% since the Iran war began. Europe is worse at a record $9.63.

This is a supply shock, not inflation. Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine knocked out regions that supply a third of the world's diesel. Russia's exports collapsed to 20% of their May level. Persian Gulf shipments fell to a quarter of prewar.

North America is filling the gap. US refiners are running flat out, and North America's share of global diesel exports just spiked to a record 23%.

Now Washington is weighing an export ban. It could pull US pump prices down for a few weeks, then spike costs for allies and push US gasoline higher.

Diesel moves your groceries and your freight. Until supply recovers, that cost stays in the system.
